portuguese-bend.place: Portuguese Bend landslide, Rancho Palos Verdes, CA
portuguese-bend.big_note: the fastest spot sank, 5 Dec 2025 to 13 Oct 2026
portuguese-bend.conclusion: The slide moved the whole time from 5 Dec 2025 to 13 Oct 2026, up to 1.3 m at its fastest spot. It sank fastest in January 2026 and slowest in September 2026. NISAR kept a reading on the slide far more often than Sentinel-1 did.
points: Between 5 Dec 2025 and 13 Oct 2026 (312 days) the fastest spot sank 127 cm.
44% of the study box sank more than 10 cm. Across that part the middle value is 50 cm.
It sank fastest in January 2026 (6.4 cm a month) and slowest in September 2026 (3.1 cm a month).
The wettest month was February 2026 (94 mm of rain), when it sank 5.8 cm. Pass by pass, speed and rain barely line up (correlation 0.17).
From 23 Nov 2025 to 17 Mar 2026, when both radars were flying, NISAR got a usable reading in the study box on 72% and 61% of passes (its two directions). Sentinel-1 got 46% and 44%.
portuguese-bend.sure: 2 GPS stations · 2 viewing directions · second radar (Sentinel-1)

central-valley.place: Central Valley subsidence near Corcoran, CA
central-valley.big_note: the fastest spot sank, 30 Nov 2025 to 8 Oct 2026
central-valley.conclusion: The ground here rose slightly through the winter and then sank steadily from February on, by 12 cm across the sinking part of the study box and 33 cm at the deepest spot by 8 Oct 2026.
points: GPS station HANF rose 2.1 cm from 30 Nov 2025 to 17 Feb 2026, then sank 8.8 cm by 8 Oct 2026.
Between 30 Nov 2025 and 8 Oct 2026 (312 days) the fastest spot sank 33 cm.
41% of the study box sank more than 10 cm. Across that part the middle value is 12 cm.
It sank fastest in March 2026 (3.7 cm a month). In December 2025 it rose instead (0.8 cm).
The wettest month was February 2026 (88 mm of rain), when it sank 1.1 cm. Pass by pass, speed and rain barely line up (correlation -0.30).
From 28 Nov 2025 to 28 Mar 2026, when both radars were flying, NISAR got a usable reading in the study box on 90% and 89% of passes (its two directions). Sentinel-1 got 82% and 86%.
central-valley.sure: 1 GPS station · 2 viewing directions · second radar (Sentinel-1)

destin.place: Hurricane Isaias landfall near Destin, FL
destin.big_note: drop in signal quality in the storm pass (landfall 10 Oct 2026 UTC)
destin.conclusion: NISAR recorded Hurricane Isaias passing: signal quality fell by 38% to 40% in the passes that span landfall (10 Oct 2026 UTC, the evening before in local time). The two viewing directions do not agree on where the ground changed, so this is evidence of the storm, not a damage map.
points: Ascending direction: average signal quality was 0.25 over the 4 calm passes before the storm, and 0.16 in the pass from 5 Oct 2026 to 17 Oct 2026, which spans landfall. That is a 38% drop.
Descending direction: average signal quality was 0.37 over the 4 calm passes before the storm, and 0.23 in the pass from 9 Oct 2026 to 21 Oct 2026, which spans landfall. That is a 40% drop.
Inside the study box on the coast, 20% of the ground changed by more than 30% in the descending direction but only 1% in the ascending one.
Only 34% of the area gives a reading in both directions. The rest is water or ground the radar could not follow.

kilauea.tag: 11 months of data · matches 15 GPS stations
kilauea.big_note: the most-changed area sank, 15 Nov 2025 to 5 Oct 2026
kilauea.conclusion: Over 324 days the ground here sank by about 14 cm in its most-changed area, and the radar matches 15 GPS stations to within about 2 cm.
points: Between 15 Nov 2025 and 5 Oct 2026 (324 days) the most-changed 1% of the area sank 13.9 cm (middle value, after averaging over about 500 m).
That area moved the same way in 16 of its 23 steps between passes.
The two viewing directions agree on where the ground moved with a correlation of 0.47 (1 would be perfect agreement, 0 none).
NISAR got a usable reading in the study box on 78% and 68% of passes (its two directions).
Against 15 GPS stations, radar and GPS differ by 2.3 cm at the typical station, and stations that moved more on GPS moved more on radar (correlation 0.73).

overall: In under a year of data, NISAR measured a landslide that sank up to 1.3 m, farmland that sank up to 33 cm, and a hurricane landfall that showed up as a loss of signal. Against Sentinel-1, its advantage was large on the steep, vegetated slide (22 percentage points more passes with a reading) and small on open farmland (5 points).
